name: Rage when wounded
summary: A passive that makes the unit hit harder the more health it has lost, either smoothly in step with its missing health or in steps below set thresholds. At full health it is ordinary; badly hurt, it is at its most dangerous, so enemies must finish it quickly or back off, and its own side must decide whether healing it is worth losing the bonus. Variants grow attack speed, life steal, regeneration, speed or damage reduction instead of or beside damage, or tie the bonus to one weapon that is weaker than standard at full health. A short boost on a key is overclock-self, and lasting ranks from kills are earn-veterancy. The levers are what grows, how steep the curve is, where it peaks and whether healing takes it away.
counterplay: Finish it in one burst: take it from healthy to dead before it can trade blows at its peak, since a badly hurt one is the most dangerous.

Kite it: most units with this passive brawl up close (the Stark fights only at short range, Lech Kos's mech is built mainly for melee and the Equalizer is a melee weapon), so keep your distance while it is wounded.
Don't trade blows when it is low: back off into your team's fire, or stun it while your team finishes it.
Make it heal out of the bonus: forcing it back to a healer or onto its own repair takes the rage away.
Switch the passive off where the game allows it: Dota's Break turns off Huskar's Berserker's Blood.

other_examples.note: Polania's resistance leader rides a mech made for close combat that can quickly close in on its targets. His passive raises his damage in step with the health he has lost: the Stark's mechanic, on a hero.

A passive that gives him faster attacks, more magic resistance and quicker health regeneration the more health he is missing; the bonuses ramp up faster as he gets lower, peak close to death, and his model grows with them. His burning spears and his leap cost his own health, so he lowers it on purpose, and Break switches the passive off.
His innate passive gives extra attack speed and lifesteal that rise as his health drops, peaking once less than a third of it remains.

sources.title: Template:Data Olaf/I (Berserker Rage), League of Legends Wiki
sources.note: The data template behind the passive's description on his page.

shooter_analogues.note: A pickaxe that does more damage the less health he has: at full health it hits softer than his other melee weapons, while near death a couple of swings can kill another Soldier. While he holds it, Medics heal him far less, so he can't stay low and be topped up at once. It first also made him faster as he got hurt; that half now sits on a separate shovel, the Escape Plan.

When his health drops below three fifths, his reload speed doubles and he turns red, giving off angry sparks; healing back above that line ends it. His other star power, Tough Guy, instead gives him a shield that cuts the damage he takes below a lower line.

shooter_analogues.game: extra:Super Smash Bros. for Wii U and 3DS / Ultimate
shooter_analogues.note: The more damage a fighter has taken, the further their attacks knock opponents back, though the damage itself does not change. It begins early and caps at a high damage level; fighters flash red and give off steam once it is strong, and in Ultimate their portrait smokes. It can help a losing player come back, but it also helps a leader survive longer, heavy fighters gain most from it, and its cheap late comebacks draw criticism.

player_translation.summary: A passive that turns the health bar into a threat meter: the lower your health, the harder you hit. You are an ordinary brawler at full health and a wrecking ball when nearly dead, so the enemy must finish you fast or back off, and your healers must choose between keeping you alive and keeping you angry.
as_user: You play close to the edge: a hurt brawler with this passive is worth more in the fight than a healthy one, so you stay in rather than retreating at half health.
You decide when to take healing: topping up ends the bonus, staying low risks dying to the next hit.
Threshold variants give one clear moment, such as reloading twice as fast below the line, which you learn to play around.
as_target: A red glow and heat haze that grows as it loses health warns you that this enemy is now at its most dangerous, much as Brawl Stars turns Bull red.
Don't trade blows with it at low health: back off, let your team's fire finish it, or stun it and burst it in one go.
Hit it from range; most raging units are brawlers.
teammates: Healers face a choice: heal it out of the bonus to keep it alive, or leave it low; Team Fortress 2 even cuts Medic healing while the Equalizer is out.
Teammates keep the enemy's long-range units off it so it can use its peak up close.
The enemy team coordinates a burst: one player stuns or slows it, another finishes it.
controls: None: the pattern is passive and spends no counted key.
The HUD shows the current bonus beside the health bar as a flame that grows, for the player and, simplified, over the unit for everyone.
feedback: A rising red glow, steam or angry sparks on the model, readable from above.
A heartbeat sound and a red edge on the user's screen as health falls, and a distinct roar when a threshold variant kicks in.
Enemies see a small flame pip over its health bar that grows with the bonus.
changes_from_rts: In Iron Harvest the bonus is a passive whose size no source gives, easy to overlook on one unit among many; a player must see and feel it, so it needs a clear meter and a visible change on the model.
An RTS unit at low health is usually pulled back; a player version must make staying in a real choice, so the peak bonus has to be big enough to matter.
Healing loops: a healer who keeps a raging unit just under a threshold exploits it, so prefer smooth ramps or put a short delay on threshold changes (proposal).
Comebacks need answers: keep the base bonus to damage alone, without damage reduction on top, so one burst still ends it.

team_play.notes: A wounded unit with this passive baits enemies into chasing a target that looks nearly dead, straight into a counterpunch and its team's fire, while the enemy needs one player to hold it and another to finish it in one go. Its own healers trade its safety against its bonus.

notes: A damage multiplier read from the health fraction, smooth or stepped.
Edge cases: healing across a threshold, damage over time near death, and stacking with other damage buffs.
Most of the work is the feedback: a meter, a glow that scales and sounds.
Comeback power feels unfair when the peak is too high; Smash's rage draws criticism for cheap late comebacks, so cap the bonus.
Self-damage plus rage (Huskar) or rage plus life steal (Olaf) can make a unit hardest to kill when it is lowest; keep sustain off the base pattern.
It also helps whoever is winning: a leader who survives long at high damage keeps the bonus, as Smash's rage does for players with a lead.
Enemies must see how angry it is; a glow that scales and a pip over the health bar keep it readable.
Exact numbers can't be read from above, so keep the curve simple: little bonus until about half health, a lot near death.

variants.name: Smooth ramp
variants.summary: Damage grows smoothly with missing health and peaks close to death.
variants.seen_in: Iron Harvest Stark (Berserk) and Lech Kos (Patriotic Frenzy)

variants.name: Threshold rage
variants.summary: One clear step: below a set share of health the unit reloads or fires much faster, and healing back above the line ends it.

variants.name: Frenzy and sustain
variants.summary: Missing health adds attack speed together with life steal or regeneration, so a low unit both hits faster and heals while it fights.
variants.seen_in: Dota 2 Huskar (Berserker's Blood), League of Legends Olaf (Berserker Rage)

variants.name: Glass weapon
variants.summary: The bonus lives on one weapon: weaker than standard at full health, deadly when low, and teammates heal its user less while it is held.

adds_weaknesses.why: At full health the weapon hits softer than standard, and while it is out teammates heal its user far less.

variants.name: Desperate speed
variants.summary: Speed instead of damage: the more hurt the unit is, the faster it moves, to escape or to chase.
variants.seen_in: Team Fortress 2 Escape Plan (the speed half of the original Equalizer)

adds_strengths.why: The more health it has lost, the faster it moves, so a wounded one is hard to catch.

variants.name: Hardens when hurt
variants.summary: Toughness instead of damage: below a threshold it takes less damage, so it is hard to finish off.
variants.seen_in: Brawl Stars Bull (Tough Guy); Dota 2 Huskar's growing magic resistance

adds_strengths.why: Below a health threshold it takes less damage, so it is hard to finish off.

variants.name: Pay to rage
variants.summary: Its own attacks or abilities cost health, so it pushes itself into the bonus on purpose.
variants.seen_in: Dota 2 Huskar (burning spears and Life Break cost his own health)

adds_weaknesses.why: Its own attacks cost health, so it can drop itself into easy reach of a finishing blow.

variants.name: Knockback rage
variants.summary: Hits push targets further back as the unit's own damage taken rises, rather than hurting more.
variants.seen_in: Super Smash Bros. rage (the fourth game and Ultimate)

adds_strengths.why: The more health it has lost, the harder it hits, so a wounded one can still turn a losing fight.

adds_weaknesses.why: At full health it gets no bonus, its peak comes when one more burst would kill it, and healing takes the bonus away.

countered_by.why: Long-range units finish it from afar instead of trading blows while it is at its most dangerous; the Stark fights only at short range and Lech Kos mostly in melee.
A stun holds it still while the enemy bursts it down, so it never swings at its peak.

open_questions: Should the bonus grow smoothly (the Stark, Lech Kos) or in steps at thresholds (Brawl Stars' Bull)? Smooth is harder to exploit, steps are easier to read.
Should teammates heal a unit less while its bonus is active, as Team Fortress 2 does while the Equalizer is out?
May a card have both this and a way to heal itself (heal-self, the heal-on-hit trait), or does that make it too hard to finish?

shooter_fit.reason: Simple to build and familiar from shooters (Team Fortress 2's Equalizer, Brawl Stars' Bull), and it makes tense low-health moments; it needs a strong visual so enemies can read the threat from above.
